abstract_sentences.text: We introduce SimuHome, a high-fidelity smart home simulator and a benchmark of 600 episodes for LLM-based smart home agents.

evidence.anchor: a benchmark of 600 episodes

abstract_sentences.relation: opens with object and benchmark scope

abstract_sentences.text: Existing smart home benchmarks treat the home as a static system, neither simulating how device operations affect environmental variables over time nor supporting workflow scheduling of device commands.

evidence.anchor: treat the home as a static system

abstract_sentences.relation: states the failure that motivates the simulator

abstract_sentences.text: SimuHome is grounded in the Matter protocol, the industry standard that defines how real smart home devices communicate and operate.

evidence.anchor: grounded in the Matter protocol

abstract_sentences.relation: moves from gap to protocol choice

abstract_sentences.text: Agents interact with devices through SimuHome’s APIs and observe how their actions continuously affect environmental variables such as temperature and humidity.

evidence.anchor: observe how their actions continuously affect environmental variables

abstract_sentences.text: Our benchmark covers state inquiry, implicit user intent inference, explicit device control, and workflow scheduling, each with both feasible and infeasible requests.

evidence.anchor: both feasible and infeasible requests

abstract_sentences.text: For workflow scheduling, the simulator accelerates time so that scheduled workflows can be evaluated immediately.

evidence.anchor: accelerates time

abstract_sentences.text: An evaluation of 18 agents reveals that workflow scheduling is the hardest category, with failures persisting across alternative agent frameworks and fine-tuning.

evidence.anchor: evaluation of 18 agents

abstract_sentences.text: These findings suggest that SimuHome’s time-accelerated simulation could serve as an environment for agents to pre-validate their actions before committing them to the real world.

evidence.anchor: could serve as an environment

abstract_sentences.relation: turns the result into a qualified deployment proposal

evidence.anchor: many everyday household requests remain beyond their reach

evidence.anchor: a manually validated benchmark of 600 episodes

introduction_moves.previous_question: How is simulator behavior turned into a broad evaluation?

evidence.anchor: workflow scheduling remains unresolved

introduction_moves.previous_question: Does the benchmark reveal a meaningful capability boundary?
introduction_moves.current_answer: Explicit control is relatively reliable, scheduling is persistent; GPT-5.1 helps at 3–5× inference time, while framework/SFT tests remain insufficient.

evidence.anchor: fundamentally different problems from smart home device control

related_work_moves.previous_question: What household tool-agent benchmark tradition exists?
related_work_moves.current_answer: 3D AI2-THOR, ALFRED, and VirtualHome emphasize navigation/manipulation, whereas SimuHome concerns networked-device APIs and environmental effects.
related_work_moves.next_hook: Move to benchmarks that target smart-home control directly.

evidence.anchor: none of these benchmarks simulates how device actions affect environmental variables over time

related_work_moves.previous_question: Which existing smart-home benchmarks are closest?
related_work_moves.current_answer: HomeBench, Sasha, and SAGE cover gold API sequences, intent interpretation, and sequential/dynamic tool use, but omit temporal environment effects, dependencies, and scheduling.
related_work_moves.next_hook: §3 specifies the simulator that fills those three gaps.

experimental_design.name: Benchmark task matrix
experimental_design.description: Six query types (QT1, QT2, QT3, QT4-1, QT4-2, QT4-3) each have feasible and infeasible variants, giving 12 categories.

evidence.anchor: yielding twelve evaluation categories in total

experimental_design.name: Episode allocation
experimental_design.description: Fifty episodes per category produce 600 total episodes.

evidence.anchor: 50 distinct episodes for each of the 12 evaluation categories
yielding 600 episodes

experimental_design.name: Initial state randomization
experimental_design.description: Layouts vary rooms/devices; all-off states undergo dependency-ordered command sampling and accelerated environment updates; a seed controls reproducibility.

evidence.anchor: Randomization is controlled by a seed to ensure full reproducibility

experimental_design.name: Goal and prerequisite contract
experimental_design.description: Each episode has initial state, structured goal, prerequisite tool calls, and natural-language query; success requires goal satisfaction plus required calls in history.

evidence.anchor: successful only if both the goal is satisfied and all prerequisite actions appear

experimental_design.name: Infeasible-condition construction
experimental_design.description: Non-existent resources, physical limits, and temporal contradictions are encoded in goals and passed to the judge.

evidence.anchor: non-existent resources
the goal records the specific condition that makes the request impossible

experimental_design.name: Query synthesis and manual validation
experimental_design.description: GPT-5 mini drafts queries from goals; two graduate students independently review and correct mismatches; Cohen’s κ is 0.92.

evidence.anchor: We used GPT-5 mini
Cohen’s κ ... was 0.92

experimental_design.name: Simulator-based evaluator
experimental_design.description: QT2/QT3/QT4 feasible episodes use exact attribute, direction, or target-time state checks plus prerequisite-history checks.

evidence.anchor: The simulator also checks that all prerequisite actions appear

experimental_design.name: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluator
experimental_design.description: All infeasible episodes and QT1-Feasible use a judge receiving goal, query, and full reasoning trajectory; three calls use majority vote.

evidence.anchor: we query the judge three times per episode and adopt the majority vote

experimental_design.name: Judge validation
experimental_design.description: A 70-episode human subset gives human κ=0.913, judge κ=0.826, and 5 misclassifications among 155 judged-incorrect cases.

evidence.anchor: Human annotators showed very high inter-rater reliability
only 5 were misclassifications

experimental_design.name: Model and framework condition
experimental_design.description: Eighteen models are evaluated in four size/reasoning groups under ReAct; OpenRouter supplies main endpoints, while two SFT variants run locally.

evidence.anchor: We evaluate 18 models across the 12 evaluation categories
The two SFT variants ... were run on local hardware

experimental_design.description: Table 1 reports category success rates; Table 2 reports average episode completion time; error taxonomies use counts and compositions.

claim_closure.claim: Static smart-home benchmarks lack temporal environmental effects, dependencies, and scheduling.
claim_closure.method_response: §3 models ticks, Matter dependencies, environmental updates, and workflows.
claim_closure.evidence_response: QT2/QT4 task definitions and Tables 1–3 operationalize the gap.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: Conclusion says static fixed sequences cannot assess the complex requests.

evidence.anchor: none of these benchmarks simulates how device actions affect environmental variables over time
static benchmarks with fixed action sequences cannot assess

claim_closure.claim: SimuHome is Matter-grounded, time-accelerated, and reproducible.
claim_closure.method_response: §3.1–§3.2 provides the three components and API semantics.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Figure 1 and Appendices A–E show the implementation contract.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: Conclusion opens by restating the interactive Matter simulator.

evidence.anchor: The simulation is fully reproducible
fully deterministic state transitions

claim_closure.claim: The benchmark contains 600 episodes across six query types and 12 feasible/infeasible categories.
claim_closure.method_response: §4.1–§4.2 defines the query matrix, goals, prerequisites, and generation pipeline.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Figure 2, Table 7, and the 50-per-category construction provide direct evidence.

evidence.anchor: yielding 600 episodes
Example goals for each query type

claim_closure.claim: Goal plus prerequisite history can be verified.
claim_closure.method_response: Structured goals, exact/direction/time checks, and required room/device queries are specified.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Figure 3 and §4.3 show simulator assertions and judge inputs.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: Conclusion refers to agents operating devices and observing resulting changes.

evidence.anchor: both the goal is satisfied and all prerequisite actions appear
direct state comparison enables fully automated and fair model-to-model comparisons

claim_closure.claim: Explicit control is relatively reliable and workflow scheduling is the most persistent challenge.
claim_closure.method_response: QT1–QT4 separate control, intent, and three scheduling forms; feedback semantics are explicit.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Table 1 and Figures 4–5 report rates and error patterns.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: Conclusion explicitly calls QT4 the most persistent challenge.

evidence.anchor: success rates (in %) across query types
workflow scheduling is the most persistent challenge

claim_closure.claim: GPT-5.1 reasoning improves scheduling but incurs a latency cost that challenges real-time use.
claim_closure.method_response: Reasoning/non-reasoning groups and average episode times are compared.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Tables 1–2 contain success and seconds values.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: Future direction calls for strong reasoning with low latency.

evidence.anchor: Average episode completion time (seconds)
three to five times longer

claim_closure.claim: Alternative frameworks and fine-tuning do not fully resolve workflow scheduling.
claim_closure.method_response: HiAgent, multi-turn, self-review, oracle, and SFT interventions test several explanations.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Figure 6 and Tables 12–14 show mixed or limited feasible-scheduling gains.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: Conclusion repeats limited SFT gains on feasible workflow scheduling.

evidence.anchor: Performance comparison between ReAct and HiAgent
limited gains

claim_closure.claim: The primary bottleneck lies in model reasoning capabilities.
claim_closure.method_response: Framework substitution, interaction, self-review, and imitation tests remove some simpler explanations.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Mixed HiAgent effects, low self-review recovery, and SFT QT4-3-F results are consistent with the claim.

evidence.anchor: primary bottleneck is not the ReAct framework but the models themselves

claim_closure.claim: SimuHome can serve as a pre-validation world model before real execution.
claim_closure.method_response: Appendix L specifies a proposed simulate–inspect–revise loop.
claim_closure.evidence_response: No deployment or agent-in-the-loop efficacy experiment is reported.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: Conclusion lists pre-validation as future work.

evidence.anchor: In a deployment scenario, the agent would execute its plan within SimuHome
could serve as an environment

claim_closure.claim: Trial-and-error inside the simulator may outperform imitation.
claim_closure.method_response: SFT tests imitation only; no trial-and-error learner is implemented.
claim_closure.evidence_response: The claim is a future direction supported indirectly by SFT’s QT4-3-F result.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: Conclusion proposes learning through trial and error.

evidence.anchor: learning through trial and error inside the simulator
static imitation alone cannot capture

claim_closure.claim: The simulator’s dynamics transfer to physical smart homes.
claim_closure.method_response: Matter-inspired dependencies and qualitative environmental effects approximate the target interface.
claim_closure.evidence_response: No physical-home transfer measurement; Appendix E explicitly calls the model simplified.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: Conclusion does not claim transfer was experimentally established.

evidence.anchor: agents developed in simulation can transfer to physical smart homes
rather than accurate physical simulation

final_judgment.single_storyline: 通过 deterministic environmental evolution 与 deferred workflow feedback，把 static smart-home benchmark 的覆盖缺口变成可复现的 QT4 scheduling 证据；pre-validation 是由该机制推出的 future proposal。
final_judgment.main_body_keeps: query matrix、goal/prerequisite contract、dual evaluator、Table 1/2、Figure 4/5，以及 feedback/framework/SFT 的决策级结果。
final_judgment.appendix_moves: API 参数、17 device types、Matter clusters、方程、goal examples、judge validation、endpoints、self-review/oracle/SFT 细节和 prompts；迁移保留正文流畅性，但增加复现跳转成本。
final_judgment.best_pattern: Figure 3 并列 simulator assertion 与 LLM judge，Figure 5 把 immediate error feedback 转成 first-try/recovered success，Table 1/2 同时给 capability 与 latency。
final_judgment.largest_gap: 没有 physical deployment/pre-validation efficacy 或 trial-and-error learner；model reasoning 的唯一瓶颈解释仍受 model family、prompt、serving 和 feedback confounding。
final_judgment.transfer_rule: 延迟执行 benchmark 应同时报告 registration feedback、execution feedback 和 recovery，并用可比 feedback 条件或 oracle upper bound 拆开机制主张与能力主张。
final_judgment.transfer_boundary: 适用于动态状态、未来执行和可验证目标的 tool/embodied agent；无未来 execution、不可观测状态或只评估最终文本时不能直接推出 simulator feedback 的因果收益。
